title: Organising
summary: Organising is the process of identifying and grouping the work to be done, defining authority and responsibility and establishing relationships so that people can work together towards goals. This chapter covers the steps and importance of organising, organisation structure (functional and divisional), formal and informal organisation, delegation and decentralisation.

notes.heading: Meaning and Steps in the Process of Organising
notes.html:
Organising is the process that initiates implementation of plans by clarifying jobs and working relationships and effectively deploying resources to achieve goals.

  1. Identification and division of work – total work is divided into manageable activities as per plans; avoids duplication and spreads the burden.
  2. Departmentalisation – similar activities are grouped together into departments (by function, product or territory).
  3. Assignment of duties – jobs are allocated to employees according to their skills and abilities (right person, right job).
  4. Establishing reporting relationships – each person knows from whom to take orders and to whom to report; creates a hierarchical structure.

Memory aid: I D A R – Identify, Departmentalise, Assign, Report.

notes.heading: Importance of Organising
notes.html:
1. Benefits of specialisation – repetitive work on one task increases skill and efficiency.
  2. Clarity in working relationships – lines of communication and reporting are clear.
  3. Optimum utilisation of resources – avoids duplication of work and wastage.
  4. Adaptation to change – structure can be modified to suit changes in the environment.
  5. Effective administration – clear description of jobs avoids confusion and duplication.
  6. Development of personnel – delegation frees managers for growth and allows subordinates to develop skills.
  7. Expansion and growth – helps the firm add new job positions, departments, products and locations.

notes.heading: Organisation Structure: Functional Structure
notes.html:
Organisation structure is the framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed. Span of management (number of subordinates a superior can manage effectively) determines the levels in the structure.

Functional structure groups jobs of a similar nature into departments such as production, purchase, marketing, finance and HR, all reporting to a coordinating head.

Suitable when: the organisation is large, has a single or few related products and requires a high degree of specialisation.

Advantages: occupational specialisation; better control and coordination within a department; helps increase managerial and operational efficiency; minimal duplication of effort; makes training of employees easier; ensures attention to all functions.

Disadvantages: functional objectives may be preferred over organisational objectives; problems in coordination between departments; conflict of interests among departments; inflexibility, since specialists have narrow perspective and are not prepared for top posts.

notes.heading: Organisation Structure: Divisional Structure
notes.html:
Divisional structure groups activities by product lines (or regions); each division has its own production, marketing, finance etc., and acts as a profit centre.

Suitable when: the organisation produces many different products requiring different skills, and when it grows and needs more employees and departments.

Advantages: product specialisation helps develop varied skills in the divisional head (prepares for top posts); accountability is clear since each division's performance can be measured (profit centre); quick decision-making as each division is semi-autonomous; facilitates expansion by adding new divisions without disturbing existing ones.

Disadvantages: conflict among divisional heads over allocation of funds; duplication of activities and resources, increasing cost; divisional heads may ignore organisational interests because of too much autonomy.

ResponsibilityDifficult to fix on a departmentEasy to fix; each division is a profit centre

notes.heading: Formal and Informal Organisation
notes.html:
Formal organisation – the structure of authority relationships deliberately designed by management to achieve goals; specifies the boundaries of authority and responsibility and follows rules. Advantages: easy to fix responsibility, no duplication, unity of command, stability. Limitations: delays (procedural rigidity), ignores social needs, does not reflect all relationships.

Informal organisation – network of social relationships that arises spontaneously when people interact at work (e.g. a group of colleagues who lunch together). Advantages: fast spread of information (grapevine), fulfils social needs, fills gaps in formal organisation, provides useful feedback. Limitations: spreads rumours, resists change, group norms may oppose organisational goals.

BasisFormal OrganisationInformal Organisation
MeaningStructure of authority created by managementNetwork of social relationships arising from interaction
OriginDeliberately created by rules and policiesArises spontaneously
AuthorityArises from positionArises from personal qualities
BehaviourDirected by rulesNo set behaviour pattern
Flow of communicationThrough the scalar chainNot through a planned route; in any direction
NatureRigidFlexible
LeadershipManagers are leadersLeaders are chosen by the group

notes.heading: Delegation of Authority
notes.html:
Delegation is the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate. The manager remains accountable for the outcome.

Elements:

  • Authority – the right to command; flows downward; arises from formal position; can be delegated.
  • Responsibility – the obligation of a subordinate to perform the assigned duty; flows upward; arises from the superior–subordinate relationship.
  • Accountability – answerability for the final outcome; flows upward; cannot be delegated.
BasisAuthorityResponsibilityAccountability
MeaningRight to commandObligation to performAnswerability for outcome
DelegationCan be delegatedCannot be entirely delegatedCannot be delegated
OriginFormal positionDelegated authorityResponsibility
FlowDownwardUpwardUpward

Importance of delegation: effective management (managers focus on important work); employee development; motivation of employees; facilitates growth; basis of management hierarchy; better coordination.

notes.heading: Decentralisation
notes.html:
Decentralisation means delegation of decision-making authority to all levels of the organisation in a systematic manner; only authority that must be exercised at the top is reserved. It is an optional policy decision. 'Everything that increases the importance of the subordinate's role is decentralisation.'

Importance: develops initiative among subordinates; develops managerial talent for the future; quick decision-making; relief to top management; facilitates growth (divisions compete); better control (performance of each level can be evaluated).

BasisDelegationDecentralisation
NatureCompulsory; work cannot be done without itOptional policy decision of top management
Freedom of actionLess; control by superiors is strongMore; less control by superiors
StatusProcess followed to share tasksResult of a policy decision
ScopeNarrow; superior to immediate subordinateWide; extends to the lowest level
PurposeLessen the burden of the managerIncrease the role of subordinates by giving more autonomy

mcqs.q: Sunrise Ltd. manufactures soaps, biscuits and paints. Each product has its own production, marketing and finance team. Which structure has it adopted?
mcqs.explanation: Grouping activities by product lines, each with its own functions, is a divisional structure.

mcqs.q: Which step of the organising process ensures that each person knows from whom to take orders and to whom to report?
mcqs.explanation: Defining superior–subordinate links is establishing reporting relationships.

mcqs.q: Which of the following cannot be delegated?
mcqs.explanation: The superior remains answerable for the outcome; accountability cannot be delegated.

mcqs.q: Employees of the accounts and sales departments formed a cricket team and spend their lunch breaks together. This is an example of:
mcqs.explanation: Spontaneous social relationships among employees form an informal organisation.

mcqs.q: In a functional structure, which of the following is a disadvantage?
options: Conflict among divisional heads over funds
Difficulty in fixing responsibility on product performance
mcqs.explanation: In a functional structure, when the firm has many products it is hard to hold any one department responsible for a product's performance. Duplication and divisional conflict are disadvantages of the divisional structure.

mcqs.q: The top management of a retail chain allowed each store manager to decide on local promotions, staff hiring and stock purchases. This is:
mcqs.explanation: Systematic dispersal of decision-making authority to lower levels is decentralisation.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Delegation is compulsory while decentralisation is optional.
Reason (R): No manager can perform all tasks alone, but dispersing authority to all levels is a policy choice of top management.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: R explains why delegation is unavoidable and why decentralisation is a policy decision.

mcqs.q: Which structure is most suitable for a large firm producing a single product and requiring high specialisation?
mcqs.explanation: A functional structure suits large firms with a single or few related products where specialisation is important.
Responsibility flows upward because a subordinate is responsible to the superior.

mcqs.q: A firm could easily add a new 'organic foods' unit without disturbing its existing units. Which advantage of divisional structure is shown?
mcqs.explanation: New divisions can be added without affecting existing ones, so the structure facilitates expansion.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): In informal organisation, communication follows the scalar chain.
Reason (R): Informal organisation arises spontaneously out of social interaction.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: A is false: in informal organisation communication has no fixed route. R is true.

mcqs.q: Grouping purchase-related activities into a purchase department and selling-related activities into a sales department is called:
mcqs.explanation: Grouping similar activities into units is departmentalisation.

questions.q: What is meant by span of management?
questions.answerHtml: Span of management is the number of subordinates that can be effectively managed by a superior.

questions.q: Which element of delegation cannot be delegated?
Explain any three points of importance of organising.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Benefits of specialisation – systematic allocation of jobs leads to repetitive work and expertise.
  2. Clarity in working relationships – it specifies who is to report to whom, removing ambiguity.
  3. Optimum utilisation of resources – proper assignment of jobs avoids duplication of work and wastage of resources.

questions.q: Explain the steps in the process of organising.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Identification and division of work – the total work is identified as per plans and divided into manageable jobs.
  2. Departmentalisation – similar activities are grouped into departments, units or sections, e.g. by function or product.
  3. Assignment of duties – jobs are allotted to members according to their skills and competence.
  4. Establishing reporting relationships – each person is told from whom to take orders and to whom to report, creating a hierarchy.

questions.q: State any four advantages of informal organisation.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Fast communication – the grapevine spreads information quickly.
  2. Fulfils social needs – members get a sense of belonging and job satisfaction.
  3. Fills gaps in formal organisation – it makes up for the shortcomings of the formal structure.
  4. Useful feedback – management can learn employees' reactions to policies through informal channels.

questions.q: Toyland Ltd. makes plastic toys in one plant and has departments for production, purchase, sales and finance. It has now decided to manufacture electronic toys and children's furniture, which require very different skills. (a) Which structure does the company have at present? (b) Which structure should it adopt now? Give two advantages and one disadvantage of the suggested structure.
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Present structure: Functional structure – activities are grouped by functions (production, purchase, sales, finance).

(b) Suggested structure: Divisional structure – since the company will have three very different product lines requiring different skills.

Advantages:

  1. Product specialisation and managerial development – each divisional head handles all functions for one product, which develops varied skills and prepares him for top posts.
  2. Easy fixation of responsibility – each division acts as a profit centre, so its performance can be measured and corrective action taken.

Disadvantage:

  • Duplication of resources – each division needs its own functional departments, which increases cost.

questions.q: Explain the elements of delegation and differentiate among them.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Authority – the right of an individual to command subordinates and take action within his area of operation. It arises from formal position, flows downward and can be delegated.

2. Responsibility – the obligation of a subordinate to properly perform the assigned duty. It arises from the superior–subordinate relationship and flows upward. Authority should be equal to responsibility.

3. Accountability – answerability for the final outcome. Once authority is delegated and responsibility accepted, the superior remains accountable; it flows upward and cannot be delegated.
